directAnswer: St. Damasus I was pope from 366 to 384, a period when Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire. He commissioned St. Jerome to revise the Latin Bible, work that led to the Vulgate, honored the martyrs with verse inscriptions in the catacombs, and strengthened the authority of the Roman see. His reign began with a violent, contested election against the rival claimant Ursinus.

paras: When Liberius died in 366, two factions chose two bishops. One group consecrated the deacon Ursinus, while a larger party elected Damasus, a deacon who had served under Liberius. Fighting broke out between their supporters, and the pagan historian Ammianus Marcellinus records that over a hundred people were killed in a single day at one of the basilicas.

The civil authorities backed Damasus and expelled Ursinus, though his followers troubled Rome for years. The episode cast a shadow over the beginning of the pontificate and was raised against Damasus by his enemies long afterward.

Around 382, the scholar Jerome came to Rome and served as Damasus's secretary. The pope asked him to revise the existing Latin translations of the Gospels, which varied widely in quality. Jerome began with the Gospels and later, after leaving Rome, went on to translate much of the Old Testament from Hebrew.

The result, known as the Vulgate, became the standard Bible of the Latin Church for more than a thousand years. A list of the books of Scripture is traditionally associated with a Roman synod Damasus held in 382, though scholars debate how much of the surviving text dates from his time.

Damasus loved the memory of Rome's martyrs. He restored their tombs in the catacombs, improved access for pilgrims, and composed Latin verse epitaphs in their honor. The calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus carved them in a distinctive and elegant lettering style.

Many of these inscriptions survive in whole or in fragments, including one in the crypt of the popes at the Catacomb of Callixtus. They are among our most important sources for several early popes and martyrs, including his predecessor Eusebius.

sections.h2: Rome's Place in an Imperial Church
paras: In 380, the emperor Theodosius I issued the Edict of Thessalonica, ordering all subjects to follow the faith handed down by St. Peter to the Romans and professed by Damasus and by Bishop Peter of Alexandria. Around the same time, Emperor Gratian stopped using the pagan title Pontifex Maximus, a gesture of distance from the old state religion.

The Council of Constantinople in 381, later counted as the second ecumenical council, met without Western participation. Damasus did not attend, but Roman synods under him condemned Arian and Apollinarian errors, and his doctrinal statements circulated widely. He also emphasized that Rome's primacy rested on the words of Christ to Peter, not on the decisions of councils.

Damasus died on December 11, 384, and was buried in a church he had built on the Via Ardeatina. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Spaniard, and Portuguese tradition associates his family with the ancient town of Egitania, today Idanha-a-Velha.

keyFacts: Pope from 366 to 384, after a violent contested election with Ursinus
Commissioned St. Jerome to revise the Latin Gospels, the start of the Vulgate
Wrote verse epitaphs for martyrs, carved by Furius Dionysius Filocalus
Named in the Edict of Thessalonica (380) as a standard of orthodox faith

faqs.question: What was Pope Damasus I's role in the Vulgate?
faqs.answer: He asked St. Jerome, his secretary, to revise the Latin Gospels around 382. Jerome's work, later extended to most of the Bible, became the Vulgate, the Latin Church's standard Scripture text for centuries.

faqs.question: What are the Damasian inscriptions?
faqs.answer: They are Latin verse epitaphs Damasus wrote for martyrs and popes buried in Rome's catacombs. Carved in a distinctive script by Filocalus, many still survive and are valuable historical sources.

faqs.question: Was Pope Damasus I from Portugal?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis describes him as Spanish, and a Portuguese tradition links his family to Egitania in Lusitania. He was probably born in Rome, where his father served as a priest.
